titleStmt.title: Making Marx More Readable: A Minimal Computing Approach to a Community-Driven Edition of Capital Vol. 1

dhq:bio.p: Avery Wiscomb is Assistant Professor of English and Digital Humanities at Virginia Tech. His research examines how computational methods reshape knowledge production in the humanities, with a focus on the institutional politics of digital scholarship and the history of computing and AI.

dhq:authorInfo.dhq:affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

dhq:bio.p: Steven Gotzler is a Teaching Assistant Professor of English and Comparative Literature and the Associate Director of the Digital Literacy and Communications Lab at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His research explores historical regimes of labor and work, cultural studies of games and play, and materialist theories of media and technology.

dhq:abstract.p: The following article presents MARXdown, a minimal digital reading edition of Karl Marx’s Capital Vol. 1, as a retrospective case study in applying minimal computing principles to create accessible, community-driven digital humanities (DH) projects. Developed by graduate students at Carnegie Mellon University in 2019–20, MARXdown demonstrates how framing minimal computing as practical commitments can lower access barriers, demystify computing labor, and facilitate knowledge sharing. The project leveraged lightweight, open-source tools to create a collaborative reading environment that addressed specific community needs. This approach allowed for adaptability during the COVID-19 pandemic, transforming MARXdown into a vital support for collaboratively reading Marx under lockdown. The article argues that practical commitments to minimal computing can promote replicable models for building digital reading editions, useful for distributing marginalized or banned texts in underserved communities. By unpacking some of MARXdown's development process, this study offers insights into both the potential and limitations of minimal computing in academic and community-driven contexts, contributing to discussions about accessibility, sustainability, and ethics in DH.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: How can digital tools enable collaborative reading and knowledge sharing for underserved communities with limited resources ? This article presents a case study of MARXdown, a minimal digital reading edition of Karl Marx's Capital Vol. 1 (1867) originally developed for graduate students at Carnegie Mellon University .

MARXdown aimed to increase access to Capital Vol. 1, enabling community annotations, and relevant commentary using accessible tools for collectively implementing a minimal reading edition online. As Roopika Risam argues, such collaborative, locally situated digital approaches can help address equity gaps and reshape the digital cultural record in academia, even with limited resources .

MARXdown's development demonstrates how minimal computing can be approached as practical commitments. By practical commitments, we refer to the concrete, actionable decisions and trade-offs made by digital humanists when applying minimal computing principles in the context of their work. Practical commitments represent the situated choices practitioners make when confronting real constraints of resources, expertise, time, and community needs. Being intentional about what these commitments are, and how we cultivate them, ensures that minimal computing principles remain rooted in embodied practice, rather than ossifying into a set of purely abstract ideals. Therefore, practical commitments emerge directly from an ongoing process that lies at the core of minimal computing: the ongoing negotiation between what is desirable and what is feasible. Throughout what follows, we use this term to emphasize how MARXdown's development involved continuous decision-making about what to prioritize, what to simplify, and what to forgo entirely—not as compromises but as affirmative choices that aligned our project with both minimal computing principles and our community's specific requirements.

These commitments reorient DH practices towards accessibility, transparency, and collaborative knowledge sharing. We argue that MARXdown, despite its obvious limitations, offers a replicable model for minimal digital reading editions. This model is valuable for sharing marginalized texts, orphan and public-domain works, or banned books in underserved communities.

MARXdown emerged from specific community needs we experienced as graduate students. Our reading group faced practical challenges: fluctuating membership as students entered and left the program, limited financial resources for purchasing multiple copies of texts, difficulties in maintaining a cohesive record of our collective engagement with Marx, and the need to reconcile different editions and translations. These constraints demanded a solution that would enable persistent yet flexible collaborative reading across changing circumstances.

As we'll discuss, these situated needs shaped our approach to minimal computing. Rather than aiming to create a comprehensive scholarly resource, we prioritized accessibility, collaborative annotation, and communal knowledge-building—essential functions for any reading community.

div.head: Background and related work
div.p: We first presented MARXdown as a generalizable model at the 2019 Cultural Studies Association (CSA) conference . A 90-minute workshop demonstrated using Jekyll for deploying static websites and the Ed. Jekyll template to create collaborative reading editions.

Comparing MARXdown to variorum editions like the Frankenstein Variorum and light-weight scholarly editions such as Walter Benjamin Digital or Electronic Beowulf, highlighted the unique community participation enabled by minimal reading editions versus complex variorum or labor-intensive scholarly editions. Feedback from presentations at other conferences such as at the Association of Computers and the Humanities and the Modern Language Association encouraged further development of the minimal computing model for digital reading editions we outline below.

Walter Benjamin Digital offers a particularly instructive comparison to MARXdown, as both projects engage with foundational theoretical texts using minimal computing principles, though with different emphases. Where Walter Benjamin Digital uses TEI-Light for encoding while maintaining a visually minimal interface, MARXdown prioritized Markdown for its lower technical barrier to entry. Both projects negotiate similar tensions between scholarly rigor and accessibility. Walter Benjamin Digital incorporates facsimile images alongside transcriptions, creating a richer documentary resource, while MARXdown focused on enhancing readability of, and collaborative engagement with, the text itself.

Our presentations at conferences revealed significant interest in minimal computing approaches that could address common challenges in graduate education and reading groups. Attendees consistently noted difficulties similar to what our group experienced: maintaining continuity amid changing membership, preserving collective knowledge, and creating accessible reading environments for texts that are often challenging both intellectually and materially to engage with. These conversations reinforced our understanding that MARXdown's design decisions—which prioritized reader experience over scholarly comprehensiveness—responded to widespread needs in academic communities.

The practical constraints that shaped MARXdown align closely with the core values of minimal computing. When faced with limited resources and specific community requirements, we found that minimal computing offered not just technical solutions but a framework for thinking about digital project development that centered accessibility and sustainability over feature richness. These considerations led us to conceptualize what we call a digital reading edition—distinct from more comprehensive scholarly editions—as will be explored in subsequent sections.

In sum, we found throughout our discussions with attendees that minimal computing principles, especially when framed as practical commitments, could help lower access barriers, facilitate knowledge sharing, and prioritize reader empowerment over back-end complexity. When put into practice, practical commitments to minimal computing can promote adaptable models for building digital reading editions that enable situated communities to engage with texts relevant to their shared contexts.

div.head: The minimal turn
div.p: Minimal computing has emerged as a significant orientation in DH, emphasizing the importance of meeting community needs within resource constraints. This approach prioritizes accessibility and sustainability over maximalist computing for its own sake, focusing on contexts of use for situated communities . However, it's important to note that such minimal work often still relies heavily on other resources such as time, goodwill, space , and technical and emotional labor .

The concept of minimal computing in DH contexts emerged in a GO::DH working group as early as 2014, although its antecedents are numerous and nebulous . At that time, the GO::DH working group defined it as computing done under some set of significant constraints of hardware, software, education, network capacity, power, or other factors, encompassing both refurbished machines for DH work out of necessity and the application of streamlined computing hardware .

head.hi: Principles and aims of minimal computing

div.p: The minimal turn in contemporary DH contexts thus far is perhaps best defined in the introduction to the Digital Humanities Quarterly (DHQ) special issue on minimal computing, edited by Alex Gil and Roopika Risam . The editors crystallize the associated principles for minimal DH projects and practitioners. We think these principles can be characterized thus:

list.item: Utilize lightweight tools (para. 6)
Environmental consciousness (para. 20)
Cultural humility about partial perspectives (para. 22)
Sustaining accessibility (para. 6–7)
Demystifying infrastructure (para. 14-15)
Avoiding uncritical dependencies (para. 12–13)

div.p: We think these principles practically aim to:

list.item: Utilizing lightweight tools (para. 6)
Curb reliance on proprietary platforms
Increase ecological and social responsibility
Demystify computing labor in the humanities
Lower participation barriers
Enhance access, freedom, and sharing of information and knowledge

div.p: At its core, minimal computing seeks to cultivate a caring habitus or way of being tailored to community needs through considerate design. By embracing accessibility and sustainability, for example, it aims to serve immediate and future users justly, while enabling more diverse participation in digitally-facilitated cultural and knowledge exchanges.

This ethos connects productively to prior concepts in IT, critical infrastructure studies, and early DH, including sustainable computing, responsible computing, green IT, and ‘poor' computing. These concepts encourage purposeful work with limited computational resources, either out of ethical or economic necessity or to intentionally experience hardware and IT restrictions others face, particularly in the Global South.Following Gil and Risam , we employ Global North and Global South as shorthand terms to describe the economic divide between high-income and low-income economies, which result largely from colonialism. We acknowledge, however, that these terms, like related concepts such as developed countries, the Third World, and the West, have limitations due to their tendency to oversimplify and their geographical vagueness.

head.hi: Practical applications in digital humanities pedagogy

div.p: In practice, minimal computing demonstrates that computers need not be cutting-edge to provide utility for DH projects. Even in STEM or data science contexts, computing can often be conducted on decade-old hardware and software with little loss in functionality. Many in the DH community have produced useful work by matching simple needs to meager hardware, IT capability, and limited technical skill sets or funding.For instance, the Pan-Africanism Data Project uses a simple Zotero group for collaborative resource management. Wearing Gay History demonstrates how minimal computing can make marginalized histories more accessible and visible. The Cyberfeminism Index showcases how a simple, text-based design can effectively present complex, specialized content. These projects, like MARXdown or Wiscomb’s democracy Journal Archive , attempt to illustrate the versatility of minimal computing principles in creating accessible, community-oriented resources, which are not necessarily synonymous with static websites .

Teaching minimal computing principles can help DH students to deliberately embrace constraints that inspire reflection on uneven barriers coded into infrastructure and prompt actions responsive to diverse accessibility challenges. For example, it can shift from an abundance narrative to one that promotes reuse and recycling of older hardware, empowering access to technology while, hopefully, reducing environmental harm .

While minimal computing offers numerous benefits in the abstract, it's important to scrutinize its implications, especially in the context of increasingly under-funded or austerity-stricken higher education:

list.item: Precarity: The turn to minimal tools or platforms risks celebrating and entrenching the already highly unstable, un- and under-compensated labor of graduate students, adjunct faculty, contract digital project workers, and Alt-Ac careers.

DIY Overload: Promoting digital practices in the humanities for their own sake can rationalize already excessive labor asked of early career scholars, students, or other workers in maximizing productivity or public-facing projects under finite resources.

Feature Creep and Worker Control: While minimal computing may start with a lean baseline, it doesn't preclude future demands for additional functionality without proper support, potentially enabling uncontrolled feature creep and worker exploitation.

De-funding Retrospective: Invoking minimal computing's virtues for sustainability and accessibility can provide convenient post-hoc cover for continued systematic and structural cuts in funding, including cuts in equipment, staffing, and other austerity measures .

div.p: If misappropriated, the minimal computing ethos in DH echoes the entrepreneurial logic of lean or agile software and startup development models popularized in the late 2000s and early 2010s . These concerns highlight how power structures can exploit the lean circumstances of an increasingly agile graduate-student workforce. The ideals of minimalism and resource constraint should not further subject vulnerable DH practitioners to austerity's consequences unless coupled with meaningful protections and renewed investment. Otherwise, exploitation dangerously compounds, or becomes super-exploitative. By super-exploitation, we refer to the condition where labor is employed at rates—and under conditions—below general remuneration levels, such that practical expectations of quality of life and job security are dangerously compromised. For example, humanities graduate students often face this reality when they are expected to perform extensive research, writing, teaching, and technical duties for DH projects for meager stipends while borrowing and accruing student debt to cover necessary living expenses for the privilege of engaging in such activities. Super-exploitation is particularly characteristic of the North American academic model, where graduate students often serve as primary instructors while receiving stipends below living wages in most metropolitan areas. Unlike some European models where doctoral candidates are more frequently employed as university staff with corresponding benefits and protections, the US system often positions graduate students in an ambiguous category between students and employees, contributing to the labor vulnerabilities we describe.

However, it's also important to note that our analysis of academic labor conditions is primarily grounded in the North American higher education context, where the casualization of academic labor, reliance on graduate student teaching, and declining tenure-track positions represent specific institutional arrangements that may differ from academic systems in other regions. While similar trends exist globally, the particular configuration of graduate labor exploitation we describe is most directly applicable to the United States and Canada.

These concerns about minimalism potentially reinforcing exploitative labor conditions connect to broader critiques in critical university studies, which have documented how academic labor has been increasingly casualized, especially in DH contexts. For example, Miriam Posner and Jacqueline Wernimont have specifically addressed the ways DH projects often rely on undercompensated graduate labor. And, as Risam and Edwards argue, DH work frequently involves invisible labor that remains uncredited and undervalued despite being essential to project success. In this context, minimal computing approaches must acknowledge what Tanya Clement [2015] calls the labor of buildingthat often falls disproportionately on those with the least institutional power.

Despite these cautionary notes, minimal computing can have other significant positive impacts. For example, it can draw attention to how financial and temporal limitations shape user experiences and interactions. It insists that claims of computational empowerment frequently overlook persisting divides across variables like class, gender, race, geography, access to technologies, and disability status . It aligns with principles of democratic participation shaped by communal needs and material realities—not merely abstract ideals of technological progress. Finally, it echoes practices like Cuban resolve—ingenious inventions under constraint that reject the capitalist logic of growth for growth's sake .

Therefore, minimal computing in DH contexts has the potential to reorient design thinking around what is minimally necessary to create, deploy, access, use, and maintain projects over time. It persistently attempts to reduce costs in terms of electricity, server space, and bandwidth, focusing on architectures of necessity .

To be clear, we don't claim to offer MARXdown as a case study which fundamentally redefines minimal computing. To the contrary, we understand our emphasis on practical commitments as offering a perspectival reminder—cautioning against the pitfalls of seeing minimal computing as a set of constraints, and instead reasserting a view of it as an active process of deliberate decision-making. This perspective matters because it foregrounds agency and intentionality in minimal computing projects, highlighting how practitioners actively engage with limitations rather than merely accepting them. For the MARXdown project, this meant approaching minimal computing not just as making do with less, but as thoughtfully determining what was necessary and sufficient for our specific community context.

div.head: Digital reading editions
div.p: Digital reading editions like MARXdown differ fundamentally from other types of digital scholarly editions in their scope, intended use, and audience. While scholarly editions often integrate paratexts, catalogs, databases, research tools, facsimile images, and more into comprehensive digital resources, reading editions prioritize accessibility and participatory experience for collaborative reading and discussion within specific communities.

Understanding distinctions between different approaches to digital editing is important for appreciating the particular role of minimal reading editions such as MARXdown. Various types of digital scholarly editions serve different purposes and face distinct challenges in the current academic landscape. These differences can be outlined briefly as follows:
Scholarly Editions(a broad category encompassing several subtypes):

list.item: Establish authoritative texts with critical apparatus, notes, sometimes competing translations, tools and historical and cultural context

May include critical editions (focused on establishing definitive text through comparison of witnesses), diplomatic editions (faithful transcriptions of source documents), facsimile editions (reproduction of original documents), genetic editions (tracing the development of a text over time), and variorum editions (presenting multiple versions over time, usually with commentary)
Often require extensive metadata and coding, though infrastructure requirements vary significantly by project
Serve advanced research purposes for scholars over general reading
Strengths: rigor, richness, scholarly authority

Weaknesses: resource-intensive, steep learning curve, increasingly precarious funding models , primarily designed for experts and specialists
Examples: The William Blake Archive, Folger Digital Texts, The Frankenstein Variorum, The Walt Whitman Archive, Mark Twain Project Online, Jane Austen’s Fiction Manuscripts
Focus on highly readable texts across platforms with minimal top-down scholarly apparatus
Use lightweight markup language and free or cheap hosting for ease of production/maintenance
Facilitate collaborative reading, annotation, and group discussion
Strengths: accessibility, flexibility, ease of engagement and deployment

Weaknesses: can lack scholarly authority, limited contextual apparatus, some technical barriers can persist
Examples: Walter Benjamin Digital, Manifold Scholarship (e.g., Debates in the Digital Humanities), democracy Journal Archive, Wearing Gay History

div.p: We propose the term digital reading editions to describe a distinct category of digital editions that prioritize collaborative reading experiences over comprehensive scholarly apparatus. Unlike established categories of digital scholarly editions that emphasize textual authority and extensive contextual materials, digital reading editions focus on accessibility, community engagement, and minimal technical requirements. By introducing this classification, we aim to highlight how lightweight, community-driven approaches to digital texts can serve different purposes than traditional scholarly editions, addressing specific needs for collaborative reading and annotation that may be overlooked in discussions focused primarily on scholarly rigor or textual authority

The concept of digital reading editions also has precedents in print culture, where publishers have long distinguished between scholarly critical editions and more accessible reading texts. In digital contexts, McGann [2001] [CITATION NOT PROVIDED] and have discussed the spectrum between scholarly and reading-oriented digital editions, though without specifically defining reading editions as an analytical category. Our formulation of digital reading editions as community-oriented, minimal computing projects represents a contribution to this taxonomy.

Therefore, while scholarly editions offer resources primarily for academic research, digital reading editions like MARXdown offer a group of readers one text they share in common for engaging with it in digital spaces, annotating it collaboratively, and discussing it across platforms.

div.head: Minimal Reading Editions and MARXdown
div.p: The MARXdown project attempted to exemplify minimal computing principles for digital reading editions in several ways. For example, it leveraged lightweight, open-source tools like Markdown, the Ed. Jekyll theme, and GitHub Pages, eschewing proprietary blogging software or complex custom website design using content management systems such as Drupal. For those unfamiliar with it, Markdown is a simple text-formatting system designed to be easy to read and write, developed in 2004 by John Gruber. Unlike complex code or word processors, Markdown uses basic symbols like asterisks for italics or hashtags for headings. It allows writers to focus on content while still creating formatted documents that can be converted to HTML for websites. Jekyll, on the other hand, transforms plain text files generated in Markdown into complete websites without requiring databases or complex programming. Think of it as a website assembler that takes content written in simple formats (like Markdown), combines it with design templates, and produces a complete website. In fact, Jekyll already powers many academic websites because it creates fast, secure sites that don't typically require expensive hosting. This style of approach to digital reading editions allowed the MARXdown project to be accessed, used, and maintained at no cost to students or community members.

Additionally, by exposing the Git-based version control system to readers, users, and future developers, MARXdown attempted to demystify its underlying infrastructure . GitHub allows users to store, share, and collaborate on code and text projects, whereas GitHub Pages is a free service that turns files stored on GitHub into public websites. This combination allows users to maintain both the source files of their project and publish them as a front-end website without additional hosting costs. Therefore, the project increased accessibility and lowered participation barriers through its use of plain-text and mobile-friendly formats, with Markdown syntax designed for readability and ease of learning, keeping technological skill requirements still fairly low. The use of Markdown syntax also ensured that MARXdown content remained readable even outside its original digital context.

While we recognized the tension in relying on Microsoft-owned GitHub—a proprietary platform that could potentially limit long-term access or change terms of service—our choice to deploy through GitHub Pages offered several sustainability advantages. This free hosting service generates static sites directly from repository content, eliminating database dependencies and reducing the technical overhead of maintenance. The infrastructure separation means that even if GitHub's policies changed, our source files would remain accessible and could be easily migrated to alternative hosting. This approach balances pragmatic use of available resources with minimal computing's concern for long-term access and reduced dependencies. Furthermore, GitHub's widespread adoption in DH communities increases the likelihood that the platform will remain accessible to academics for the foreseeable future, while its version control system creates transparency about the development.

In sum, MARXdown's commitments to minimal computing principles result in a digital reading edition that is accessible, sustainable, and transparent. The project demonstrates how such guidelines, when applied in real-world contexts, can be effectively implemented in DH initiatives, balancing the benefits of minimal computing with awareness of its potential pitfalls.

div.head: The MARXdown project
div.p: MARXdown was initially developed to make Marx's Capital Vol. 1 accessible for reading, annotation, and asynchronous discussion. Designed for CMU graduate students and adjacent community members without extensive scholarly background or computing resources, it attempts to operationalize the principles of minimal computing in a digital reading edition:

list.item: Focused Content: Presents a basic, readable version of the text in straightforward translation, preserving Marx’s footnotes and links to his sources but excluding comprehensive scholarly apparatus or analytical tools.
Simple Infrastructure: Utilizes simple annotation, free hosting, and preexisting web tools to enable collaborative annotation and asynchronous reading group functionality.
Community-Oriented: Design choices reflect the specific needs of the intended readership, prioritizing accessibility and reading-group engagement over expansiveness.
Participatory Interpretation: Fosters collaborative reading of a difficult text itself rather than preserving or studying textual variants, alternate translations, or archival material.
Resource Consideration: Demonstrates respect for readers' and creators' time and resources by keeping the edition simple, flexible, and focused on facilitating readability and discussion.

div.p: The tradeoffs involved in opting for accessibility over expansiveness were viewed as justified, given MARXdown's aim to foster participatory interpretation and collaborative reading among the graduate students at CMU and other U.S. universities. This approach provides sufficient context for appreciating the core text without pursuing maximalist technologies for their own sake.

In sum, digital reading editions like MARXdown offer a focused, accessible approach to engaging with texts in digital spaces. By prioritizing readability and discussion over comprehensive scholarly apparatus, they can serve as valuable tools for fostering community engagement with important works, particularly in contexts where resources or specialized technical knowledge may be limited.

The necessity for a digital reading edition of Capital Vol.1 grew out of our involvement with the Contemporary Marxist Reading Group at Carnegie Mellon University (CMRG-CMU).Although organized by Gotzler and Wiscomb , MARXdown was developed with other input from CMRG-CMU members: Natalie Suzelis, Christopher Wike, Jacob Goessling, Corbin Hiday, and Marah Nagelhout. Special acknowledgement goes to Alex Gorman for creating the annotation style guide and Chloe Perry for preparing and uploading prefaces and afterwords from various Capital Vol. 1 editions. The dSHARP lab at Carnegie Mellon University Libraries, including at different times Daniel Evans, Jessica Otis, Matthew Lincoln, and Scott Weingart, provided crucial technical support to overcome project bottlenecks (see n. 5). For more on Carnegie Mellon Library Labs, see . Primarily, the MARXdown project was driven by the material constraints common to the graduate students who organized the group. Formed in 2014, the group initially consisted of PhD and MA students in the Literary and Cultural Studies program at Carnegie Mellon University, to continue our engagement with Marx and Marxist theory as we transitioned out of coursework into dissertation writing.

However, over time, the CMRG-CMU developed as a space for encouraging the study of contemporary Marxist theories on campus but also more broadly. For example, the group helped organize the campus-wide, year-long Marx@200, events in 2017-2018, featuring talks by Jodi Dean, Kathi Weeks, and others. Additionally, CMRG-CMU facilitated connections between students at regional and other institutions like the University of Pittsburgh, Duquesne University, Yale University, and Brown University, and local political organizations such as the Pittsburgh Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and Socialist Alternative (SA).

In 2016, Gotzler co-organized and led a Capital Vol. 1 summer reading group with other CMRG-CMU members. Leaning heavily on David Harvey’s lectures (in both podcast and YouTube format), the group first read through Marx’s text over 13 weeks. The discussions and debates that took shape during this summer-camp effort allowed the group to generate its own situated reading of Marx’s important, but often under-read and under-taught, book. This situated reading blended the group’s unique mix of intellectual interests and reflected the particularities of our socially located experiences.

Our initial reading engaged with several critical debates and contemporary issues, deeply rooted in our academic interests and labor context at the time. We explored topics ranging from the transition from feudalism to capitalism in early modern studies to the ecological transformations of the Middle Ages. Simultaneously, we examined Pittsburgh's history through the lens of its gentrifying urban spaces within the post-industrial Appalachian landscape. These historical perspectives resonated with our position as graduate students, experiencing casualization and exploitation within the U.S. university system. As Marc Bousquet evocatively phrased it, we were becoming the university's soon-to-be waste products [2002]. This unique vantage point allowed us to draw connections between historical processes and the contemporary socio-economic challenges we faced as graduate students.
